Goals are the second section of the roadmap. They are the evidence we look for to know the vision and strategy are working: changes in what people do, measured against a starting point and a target. The vision says where we're headed and the strategy says how we'll choose. Goals tell us whether we're actually getting there.

## When

- **Set yearly**, during step 2 of the process flow, Set direction. A goal covers one to two years. At the yearly direction review, each goal is kept, revised or retired.
- **Progress is updated quarterly**, during step 3, Plan the quarter. Before the team commits to new work, the product manager fills in the goal progress table with fresh numbers.
- **Goal progress is not updated each sprint.** The sprint report tracks deliverables. Behavior change moves too slowly to read every two weeks, and reading it that often turns noise into false alarms. The team can look at its data whenever it wants. The official update happens once a quarter.

## Who

- **Executive steering group** sets the goals with the product manager each year and approves the targets. Leadership owns what success means. The team owns how to get there.
- **Product manager** leads. They draft the goals, set the baselines, gather the numbers each quarter, update the table and explain what changed.
- **Advisory group** gives context on what matters to the community and to partner agencies, and checks that the goals match those priorities.
- **UX designer and researcher** help design the measures, especially ones that need surveys or observation, such as staff satisfaction.
- **Technical architect and development team** build in the analytics needed to measure the goals, and flag measures that can't be collected.
- **Product owner** connects each sprint's work to the goals during refinement, so the team knows which goal a story serves.

## How it works

1. **Start from problems.** At the yearly session, the steering group and product manager list the problems the service should solve. Each person writes their own list in silence first, then the group sorts and discusses. Next they ask: if we solved these, what would that look like? Who would it affect? What would those people do differently? This is the Leadership Product Workshop sequence (problems, objectives, people affected, behavior change).
2. **Write each goal as a behavior change.** Use the format: *By [timeframe], [user group] will [behavior change], measured by [metric], creating [community value].* Keep it to three goals or fewer. Two should be public-facing. The third may be an internal goal, like staff experience, when it makes better public service possible.
3. **Set baseline and target.** Record where the measure stands today in the Started column. If no data exists yet, write "Baseline" and plan how you'll collect it in the first quarter. Targets should be ambitious. Reaching most of the way there in two years counts as real progress.
4. **Each quarter, update the table.** At quarterly planning, the product manager moves the old Current value into Last, enters the new reading as Current, and sets the progress circle.
5. **Set intended progress for the coming quarter.** In the Quarterly commitments section, each goal gets **intended progress**: a short milestone name and one line saying what we will be able to show by the end of the quarter, given the deliverables we're committing to. Use movement on the goal measure when you can. When the measure can't move yet because nothing has reached users, name evidence that we're on the way, with a number: "25 beta users complete renewals end to end", not "renewal is built".
6. **Judge progress against intended progress.** Next quarter, compare the new Current value with the intended progress line from last quarter, not with the final target. A goal at 0% is fine in a quarter when nothing has shipped, as long as we said so. A goal that should have moved and didn't needs a conversation.

**Intended progress** is the team's bet for the quarter. **Goal progress** is what the data says afterward. The gap between them is the most useful thing the roadmap shows the steering group.

### Progress circles

| Circle | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Grey | Starting, no data yet, or no movement expected this quarter |
| Green | At or ahead of intended progress |
| Yellow | Behind intended progress |
| Red | Moving the wrong way, or the measure has stopped working |

Progress circles are for goals only. Deliverables in Quarterly commitments use the status labels Committed, On track, Off track and Done.

## Template
Use [goal.md](/templates/goal) for each goal statement. The goal progress table is section 2 of [roadmap.md](/templates/roadmap), and the intended progress card is in section 4.

## DMV example
**Goal statements**

| Short name | Goal |
|---|---|
| 75% of renewals online within 5 minutes | By the end of fiscal year 2028, Oregon vehicle owners will renew their registration online in under 5 minutes instead of an average of 45 minutes in an office, measured by the share of all renewals completed online in under 5 minutes (target 75%), creating time back for residents and shorter lines for those who need a visit. |
| Zero multi-trip experiences for standard licenses | By the end of fiscal year 2028, applicants for a standard new driver license will finish in a single interaction, measured by the share of applications needing more than one office visit (target 0%), ending the "bring documents and hope" experience. |
| 30% staff satisfaction improvement | By the end of fiscal year 2028, DMV counter staff will spend their time solving complex cases instead of processing routine transactions, measured by the staff satisfaction survey (target +30% over baseline), creating a workforce that can help the people who most need it. |

**Goal progress, Q1 planning update:** see section 2 of the DMV example in [roadmap.md](/templates/roadmap). Two goals are Grey; staff satisfaction is Green at +5% against a +30% target.

**Intended progress, Q1 commitments**

| Goal | Intended progress this quarter | Initiative: Deliverables that drive it |
|---|---|---|
| Renewals online | **Service ready.** Online renewal working, with 25 beta users completing renewals end to end. The goal measure won't move until the wider launch in Q2. | Online vehicle renewal: Backend Integration, User Interface |
| Single-trip licenses | **Infrastructure proven.** Digital identity verification at 99% uptime in production with real DMV data, which makes real-time eligibility checks possible. | Real-time eligibility verification: Digital Identity Verification System |
| Staff satisfaction | **Staff ready.** 10 frontline staff can show they're able to guide residents through the new online process. | Counter staff on complex cases: Staff Training Program |

At Q2 planning, the product manager will check the Staff Training Program, which is Off track in Q1. If fewer than 10 staff are ready and the satisfaction survey stalls, the circle goes yellow, and the steering group sees both the slipped deliverable and the effect on the goal together.

## Rules of thumb

- **Measure people, not features.** "Automate 90% of permit types" is an output. "Residents get a permit decision in half the time" is a goal. If the goal is just a list of things to build, rewrite it.
- **Watch for either/or services.** When residents have no choice, such as a single renewal system, "convert 25% of users" makes no sense. Measure completion, time or repeat trips instead.
- **Three goals, held one to two years and reviewed yearly.** Changing goals each quarter tells the team the strategy is not real.
- **Goals are not a performance review.** Tie them to people's evaluations and targets will shrink to what is safe.
- **Commitments are promises. Goals are bets.** Hold the team accountable for deliverables and honest measurement, and use missed goals to learn.
- **No baseline, no goal.** If you can't measure where you are today, collecting that number is the first quarter's intended progress.
